*How do you build a manifold whose true geometry you already know?*

## What this chapter answers {#bench-question}

A benchmark for dimension reduction has to supply four things. Three of them are
routine. Data: points in an ambient space that a method can be handed. A
difficulty axis: some parameter that makes the same object harder without making
it a different object. An answer key: the coordinates the method should have
recovered. The Swiss roll and its relatives supply all three, and so does every
folded sheet in this book.

The fourth is the one that is almost never supplied, and it is what this chapter
builds. **How much of the error was unavoidable?** A method that scores an error
of one half on a dataset has either thrown away most of the structure or reached
the limit of what two dimensions can hold, and the score alone does not say
which. Without that number a benchmark can rank methods against each other but
cannot say whether any of them did well, and a ranking with no scale under it is
how a survey ends up reporting that every method is mediocre on every dataset
[@espadoto2021survey].

The number exists and is computable in closed form, but computing it needs a
manifold whose intrinsic dimension exceeds the target. That is this chapter's
argument: the constructions in `R/constructions.R` exist to raise intrinsic
dimension while keeping the answer key exact, because a chart of dimension two
embedded into dimension two has an irreducible loss of exactly zero and nothing
to say.

The chapter also records what the benchmark does *not* contain. Two pattern
families were specified for it and both were withdrawn on evidence, and they are
reported here as results — what it takes for a pattern to qualify is worth more
to a reader than a list of the ones that did.

## Setup {#bench-setup}

```{r bench-setup-chunk, echo=TRUE}
grid <- read_run("data/processed/product-grid.rds", "bb8ade76d88b95a3")
fac_a <- miura_ori(4L, 4L, alpha = pi / 3)
fac_b <- miura_ori(3L, 5L, b = 1.4, alpha = pi / 4)
```

`grid` is the product suite, `r nrow(grid)` rows produced by
`scripts/run-product-grid.R`; `fac_a` and `fac_b` are the two factors it is
built from. Everything else this chapter calls is in `R/`, sourced when the book
renders.

## Background {#bench-background}

### Four objects, four verbs

The helper API is small on purpose. Three S3 classes carry everything between
files, each a plain list, and `R/README.md` states the contract field by field.

A **`crease_pattern`** is a flat, unfolded pattern: vertices in the plane,
facets as vertex-index cycles, and a crease table carrying a
mountain/valley/boundary assignment. Its `vertices` matrix is the ground truth —
not an approximation of the correct two-dimensional embedding, the embedding
itself.

A **`folded_pattern`** is the same pattern placed in $\mathbb{R}^3$ at folding
parameter $\theta$, with one dihedral angle per crease derived from the
placement rather than assumed.

A **`manifold_sample`** is $n$ points drawn from a folded pattern: `X` in the
ambient space, `truth` in the chart, row-aligned. `X[i, ]` and `truth[i, ]` are
the same point seen two ways, and every measurement in this book compares an
embedding of the first against the second. The verbs run one line each.

```{r bench-api, echo=TRUE}
p  <- miura_ori(nx = 6L, ny = 6L, alpha = pi / 3)
s  <- sample_manifold(p, theta = 0.6, n = 400L, seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1])
Y  <- embed("isomap", s, d = EMBED_DIM, k = K_DEFAULT)
data.frame(vertices = nrow(p$vertices), creases = nrow(p$creases),
           points = nrow(s$X), ambient = ncol(s$X), chart = ncol(s$truth),
           error = round(reconstruction_error(Y, s$truth), 4))
```

Four things about that call are load-bearing and easy to get wrong.

$\theta$ **is a parameter of the folding map, not an angle.** It runs on
$[0, 1]$, zero being the flat sheet and one the flat-folded state, and `fold()`
refuses anything outside it; the dihedral angles are derived from it. Chapter
\@ref(folding-geometry) gives the derivation.

`embed()` **takes the sample object, not a matrix.** The registry holds
`r length(METHOD_REGISTRY)` entries and
`r sum(vapply(METHOD_REGISTRY, function(s) is.null(s$unavailable), logical(1)))`
of them run: the autoencoder declares itself unavailable rather than failing at
fit time, and `method_table()` prints the registry with what each method
consumes.

**Stochastic methods refuse to run unseeded.** Standing rule 1 reports every
stochastic result across `BENCH_SEEDS`, and an unseeded fit cannot be one of
them, so `embed()` errors rather than quietly producing an anecdote.

**Sampling trims the boundary by default.** The chart is the geodesic only while
the straight chart segment between two points stays on the paper, and a Miura
unfolds to a region with a zigzag edge. `boundary = FALSE` is not tidiness — it
is the condition under which the answer key is the answer.

## Constructions that keep the answer key {#bench-core}

### One pattern family, and two honest gaps

The book ships one family that folds. That is fewer than were specified, and the
two that were withdrawn were withdrawn for different reasons, both of which are
worth more than the families would have been.

```{r bench-fig-families, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Two valid flat crease patterns. Only the left one has a certified rigid folding; the right one is drawn here and never folded anywhere in this book. Mountain and valley are distinguished by colour and by line style together.", fig.alt="Two side-by-side panels of flat crease patterns drawn in the plane. The left panel is a Miura-ori: a grid of congruent parallelograms whose transverse crease lines zigzag, with a jagged left and right edge. The right panel is a Yoshimura diamond tessellation: rows of triangles with horizontal, slanted and diagonal creases meeting six to a vertex. Both use two colours and two line styles for mountain and valley creases and a solid grey line for the sheet boundary."}
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
  plot_crease_pattern(fac_a, title = "A  Miura: builds, and folds"),
  plot_crease_pattern(yoshimura(6L, 6L),
                      title = "B  Yoshimura: builds, and does not fold"),
  ncol = 2)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:bench-fig-families) shows the Miura beside the Yoshimura. Both
panels are legitimate crease patterns. `yoshimura()` returns a `crease_pattern`
like any other, its facets are congruent, and its interior vertices satisfy
Kawasaki's condition — the alternating sum of the sector angles vanishes — to
numerical noise. What it does not have is a folding.

```{r bench-refusals, echo=TRUE}
yo <- yoshimura(6L, 6L)
kaw <- max(vapply(interior_vertices(yo), function(v) {
  a <- sector_angles(yo, v)
  abs(sum(a[c(TRUE, FALSE)]) - sum(a[c(FALSE, TRUE)]))
}, numeric(1)))
first_line <- function(e) sub("\\. See .*", ".", conditionMessage(e))
refusals <- c(
  yoshimura = tryCatch(fold(yo, theta = 0.5), error = first_line),
  waterbomb = tryCatch(waterbomb(), error = first_line))
cat(strwrap(refusals, width = 76, prefix = "  ", initial = ""), sep = "\n")
```

Kawasaki's alternating sum is satisfied at all
`r length(interior_vertices(yo))` interior vertices of that patch, worst
departure `r format(signif(kaw, 2), scientific = TRUE)`, and that buys
nothing. Kawasaki is a necessary condition for flat-foldability at a vertex; it
is not sufficient, and
flat-foldability of a pattern is not the same question as the existence of a
one-parameter rigid folding of a tessellation [@hull2020origametry;
@demaine2007folding].

**The Yoshimura.** Two rigid foldings of the planar patch were derived,
implemented and verified in this repository. Each of them is exact — facet
isometry at the same order as the Miura's, flat at $\theta = 0$ — and each
leaves one of the three crease families entirely unfolded, at a dihedral angle
of $\pi$ along its whole length. A folding that leaves a crease family flat is a
folding of a coarser pattern: fuse the facets across the creases that never
move, and what remains is a parallelogram tessellation. It is a Miura wearing
the Yoshimura's crease lines. Shipping it as a second, independent family would
have been a claim about pattern variety that the geometry does not support, so
`fold()` refuses it and says why.

**The waterbomb.** `waterbomb()` stops before building anything. A degree-six
vertex with sectors of forty-five, forty-five and ninety degrees repeated
satisfies Kawasaki and is flat-foldable *as an isolated vertex*, which does not
imply that the tessellation admits a one-parameter rigid folding. Whether it
does is an open question in this project, not a coding task. A continuation
moved it only under an imposed symmetry, and three things disqualified that
result: the embedding is unproved, the fold amplitude is not monotone in
$\theta$, and degrees of freedom remain on the free boundary, so $\theta$ does
not determine the configuration.

Both withdrawals share one moral and it generalises well past origami. **A test
that a correct implementation passes is not the same as a test that a wrong one
fails.** An isometry check cannot tell a fold from a pleat, because a pleat is a
rigid folding and passes perfectly. A first-order flex at the flat state proves
nothing either: at $\theta = 0$ every $z$ column of the rigidity Jacobian
vanishes, so the count of non-trivial infinitesimal flexes is
$V - 3 = `r nrow(p$vertices) - 3L`$ for a pattern of this size and for *any*
planar pattern whatsoever, foldable or not. Each trap here was sprung, and each
was caught only by a second, independent check.

### The isometry certificate

What a family has to produce, then, is a closed form, a fold that reaches every
crease family, and an isometry that is exact rather than converged. The third is
certified by measurement, not by the derivation that produced it.

```{r bench-certificate, echo=TRUE}
alphas <- seq(MIURA_ALPHA_RANGE[1], MIURA_ALPHA_RANGE[2], length.out = 6L)
thetas <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.05)
cert <- do.call(rbind, lapply(alphas, function(al) {
  q <- miura_ori(4L, 4L, alpha = al)
  data.frame(alpha = round(al * 180 / pi), theta = thetas,
             err = vapply(thetas, function(t) facet_isometry_error(q, t),
                          numeric(1)))
}))
worst <- max(cert$err)
```

`facet_isometry_error()` compares **all pairwise distances** between a facet's
vertices, folded against flat, and not merely its edges: a placement that
preserved every edge of a parallelogram while shearing it would pass an edge
test and would not be a rigid folding. Over the whole $\theta$ sweep and the
full $\alpha$ range the worst departure is
`r format(signif(worst, 2), scientific = TRUE)`, against a contract of
`r format(TOL$isometry, scientific = TRUE)`. That is floating-point noise on a
closed form, not a tolerance anyone chose, and it is the certificate the product
construction below inherits.

```{r bench-fig-certificate, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Worst within-facet distance error across the folding sweep, at six opening angles spanning the range the contract asserts. The dashed line is the contract; every curve sits five orders of magnitude below it and shows no trend in either the folding parameter or the opening angle.", fig.alt="A line chart with a logarithmic vertical axis. The horizontal axis is the folding parameter from zero to one. Six nearly flat curves, one per opening angle and distinguished by colour, sit together in a narrow band around ten to the power minus fifteen. A horizontal dashed line far above them at ten to the power minus ten marks the contract tolerance."}
ggplot2::ggplot(cert, ggplot2::aes(theta, pmax(err, 1e-18),
                                   colour = alpha, group = alpha)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = TOL$isometry, linetype = "dashed",
                      colour = "grey40") +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_book_c(name = "opening angle (degrees)") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = expression(theta),
                y = "worst within-facet distance error") +
  theme_fold()
```

Figure \@ref(fig:bench-fig-certificate) is that measurement across the sweep.
The flatness matters as much as the level: an error growing with $\theta$ would
mean the closed form was an approximation that happened to be good near the flat
state, which is what a derivation by facet rotation tends to produce.

### Products: raising intrinsic dimension without losing truth

A folded sheet has intrinsic dimension two and every embedding in this book has
target dimension two. That is a benchmark with no headroom, and the product
construction supplies some.

`product_manifold(a, b)` takes two samples of the same size and pairs them
row-wise: the ambient coordinates concatenate to $\mathbb{R}^{3+3}$, the charts
to $\mathbb{R}^{2+2}$. Nothing is fitted and nothing approximated, for a reason
worth stating because everything downstream rests on it.

**A product of isometries is an isometry.** In a Riemannian product the squared
distances add: for points $(u, v)$ and $(u', v')$,
$d^2 = d_1(u, u')^2 + d_2(v, v')^2$, and the same identity holds in the ambient
product because concatenating coordinate blocks adds squared differences. Each
factor map preserves its own term by construction, so the product map preserves
the sum. The chart of the product is therefore the product of the charts, exactly, and
its intrinsic dimension is the sum of the factors' — $2k$ in ambient $3k$ for
$k$ sheets.

```{r bench-product, echo=TRUE}
sa <- sample_manifold(fac_a, theta = 0.55, n = 400L, seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1])
sb <- sample_manifold(fac_b, theta = 0.60, n = 400L, seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1] + 500L)
pr <- product_manifold(sa, sb)

pythag <- max(abs(as.matrix(dist(pr$truth)) -
                  sqrt(as.matrix(dist(sa$truth))^2 + as.matrix(dist(sb$truth))^2)))
floors <- vapply(1:4, function(d) irreducible_loss(pr, d), numeric(1))
data.frame(ambient = ncol(pr$X), chart = ncol(pr$truth),
           pythagoras = formatC(pythag, format = "e", digits = 1),
           one_sheet_floor = irreducible_loss(sa, 2L))
```

The Pythagorean identity holds to `r format(signif(pythag, 2), scientific = TRUE)` across all pairs, which
is the numerical form of the argument above. The last entry is the sentence the
whole construction exists to escape: a single folded sheet has a chart of
dimension two, and the smallest error any two-dimensional embedding of it could
achieve is `r irreducible_loss(sa, 2L)`. Exactly zero, in every cell, at every
$\theta$, under every noise model.

**The bound.** For an $n \times p$ chart $U$ and the normalised Procrustes error
of `R/metrics.R` — which optimises over translation, rotation, reflection and
isotropic scale [@schonemann1966procrustes; @gower1975procrustes] — every
$n \times d$ configuration $Z$ satisfies

$$\mathrm{err}(Z, U) \;\ge\; \mathrm{floor}(d) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i > d}\lambda_i}{\sum_i \lambda_i}},$$

where the $\lambda_i$ are the classical-MDS eigenvalues of the chart
[@torgerson1952mds], equivalently the squared singular values of its centred
coordinates. The proof is Eckart–Young [@eckart1936approximation] and it is
short. As $Z$ ranges over all configurations and the similarity group ranges
over its elements, the fitted matrix ranges over exactly the centred $n \times p$
matrices of rank at most $d$; the best such matrix is the rank-$d$ truncated
singular value decomposition; its residual is the tail sum of squared singular
values; normalising gives the expression above.

It is exact, it depends on the data alone, and no method appears anywhere in it.

```{r bench-fig-spectrum, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4, fig.cap="The chart spectrum of one product cell, and the bound it produces. Panel A: the four eigenvalues of the four-dimensional chart, as shares of its variance. Panel B: the bound at each target dimension, as a line, with the rank-d projection of the chart drawn on top of it as crosses. The tail of A is the square of B.", fig.alt="Two panels. Panel A is a bar chart of four bars, decreasing from about 0.43 to about 0.06, labelled as shares of chart variance. Panel B is a line falling from about 0.75 at target dimension one, through 0.53 and 0.25, to zero at target dimension four; black cross markers sit exactly on the line at all four points."}
lam <- chart_spectrum(pr$truth)
Uc  <- sweep(pr$truth, 2L, colMeans(pr$truth))
sv  <- svd(Uc)
att <- vapply(1:4, function(k)
  reconstruction_error(Uc %*% sv$v[, seq_len(k), drop = FALSE], pr$truth),
  numeric(1))
pA <- ggplot2::ggplot(data.frame(k = seq_along(lam), share = lam / sum(lam)),
                      ggplot2::aes(factor(k), share)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = "grey78", colour = "grey30", width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "chart eigenvalue", y = "share of chart variance",
                title = "A  The spectrum") + theme_fold()
pB <- ggplot2::ggplot(data.frame(d = 1:4, floor = floors, attained = att),
                      ggplot2::aes(d, floor)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = "grey25") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(y = attained), shape = 4, size = 3,
                      stroke = 1.2) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "target dimension d", y = "normalised Procrustes error",
                title = "B  The bound, and a configuration on it") + theme_fold()
gridExtra::grid.arrange(pA, pB, ncol = 2)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:bench-fig-spectrum) shows why it is a bound rather than a
guess: **it is attained.** The crosses in panel B are the chart projected onto
its own top $d$ principal directions, scored by the same function every method
in the book is scored by. They sit on the line, to
`r format(signif(max(abs(att - floors)), 2), scientific = TRUE)`. A minimum, not an infimum — which also
makes clear what the bound is not. The minimiser is constructed from the answer
key, so nothing that has not been given the answer can be expected to reach it.

The floor depends on the chart and on nothing else. That is the property that
makes it useful rather than a limitation: it does not move with $\theta$, with
the noise model or with the sample's difficulty, so "every method landed within
a few per cent of the floor" is a statement about a regime rather than about a
lucky draw.

### Lifting to arbitrary ambient dimension

Real data does not arrive in three dimensions, and a method that only works when
the ambient dimension is small should be caught by that rather than flattered by
it. `lift()` maps a sample into $\mathbb{R}^D$ through a random orthonormal
matrix.

```{r bench-lift, echo=TRUE}
lf <- lift(pr, D = 50L, seed = 20260901L)
dist_change <- max(abs(as.matrix(dist(lf$X)) - as.matrix(dist(pr$X))))
data.frame(ambient = ncol(lf$X),
           dist_change = formatC(dist_change, format = "e", digits = 1),
           floor_before = round(irreducible_loss(pr, 2L), 4),
           floor_after  = round(irreducible_loss(lf, 2L), 4))
```

Orthonormality is load-bearing and `lift()` asserts it rather than assuming it:
a merely random matrix would distort distances and invalidate the answer key
silently. Because $Q^\top Q = I$ the map is exactly distance-preserving — the
worst change over all
`r format(choose(nrow(pr$X), 2))` pairs is
`r format(signif(dist_change, 2), scientific = TRUE)` — and the
chart is untouched, so the floor is the same number before and after.

That decoupling is the point. Ambient dimension and intrinsic difficulty are two
axes, and a benchmark that moves them together cannot say which a method is
responding to. `lift()` moves the first alone.

## Results {#bench-results}

The product suite is `r nrow(grid)` rows: two arms, each swept over nine values
of its own difficulty parameter, `r length(unique(grid$seed))` seeds, four target
dimensions and `r length(unique(grid$method))` registry entries at
$n = `r attr(grid, "provenance")$n`$.

The second arm is a concession turned into a finding. `PROJECT_CONCEPT.md`
listed crease-specificity among the book's differentiators, and
`product_manifold()` imposes no family constraint: two isometric Swiss rolls
give intrinsic dimension four, an exact chart and a computable floor exactly as
two Miura sheets do. The differentiator as written is refuted, and reporting
both arms side by side is the stronger statement. What crease-specificity rests
on afterwards is zero reach [@federer1959curvature; @niyogi2008homology] and an
answer key that is not smooth, not the bound.

### The floor bites, and nothing goes under it

```{r bench-fig-dimension, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Achieved error against target dimension, by what each method consumes, with the irreducible-loss bound as the heavy line and the region below it shaded. Both arms have a four-dimensional chart, so the bound reaches zero at target dimension four. The shaded region is unreachable by any configuration whatsoever.", fig.alt="Two panels sharing a vertical axis of normalised Procrustes error from zero to one. In each, a heavy grey line falls with target dimension one to four and the area beneath it is shaded. In the left panel, labelled crease product, three curves for ambient, geodesic and neighbourhood methods run just above the shaded region at dimensions one and two and separate from it at three and four. In the right panel, labelled roll product, the same three curves run flat near 0.95 across all four dimensions, far above a bound that falls quickly to near zero."}
ok  <- grid[grid$ran, ]
arm <- c(crease = "crease product: two Miura sheets",
         roll   = "roll product: two Swiss rolls")
by_d <- aggregate(rmse ~ consumes + d + family, ok, mean)
by_d$arm <- arm[by_d$family]
fl_d <- aggregate(floor ~ d + family, ok, mean)
fl_d$arm <- arm[fl_d$family]
ggplot2::ggplot(by_d, ggplot2::aes(d, rmse, colour = consumes,
                                   linetype = consumes, shape = consumes)) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(data = fl_d,
                       ggplot2::aes(x = d, ymin = 0, ymax = floor),
                       inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey86") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(data = fl_d, ggplot2::aes(d, floor), inherit.aes = FALSE,
                     linewidth = 1, colour = "grey25") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ arm) +
  viridis::scale_colour_viridis(discrete = TRUE, option = BOOK_VIRIDIS_OPTION,
                                end = 0.75) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "target dimension d", y = "normalised Procrustes error") +
  theme_fold()
```

```{r bench-unbeaten, echo=TRUE}
fits <- nrow(ok)
under <- sum(ok$excess < -1e-9)
crease2 <- ok[ok$d == 2L & ok$family == "crease", ]
roll2   <- ok[ok$d == 2L & ok$family == "roll", ]
by_con <- aggregate(excess ~ consumes, crease2, mean)
```

Across all `r fits` fits in the suite, the number that went under the floor is
`r under`. That is a regression check and not evidence, and the distinction
matters: the bound is
*proved*, so a method that beat it would mean the implementation is wrong, not
that the claim is. It is the assertion the producer exits non-zero on, and it
should be read the way a failing test is read, not the way a corroborated
conjecture is.

Figure \@ref(fig:bench-fig-dimension) is what the bound buys. At target
dimension two the crease arm's floor is
`r signif(mean(crease2$floor), 3)`: the best configuration that exists still
leaves a residual half the size of the chart's own spread, before any method is
chosen. Isomap's raw error there averages
`r signif(mean(crease2$rmse[crease2$method == "isomap"]), 3)`, which against
zero reads as failure and against the floor is an excess of
`r signif(mean(crease2$excess[crease2$method == "isomap"]), 3)` — it gives away
`r signif(100 * mean(crease2$gave_away[crease2$method == "isomap"]), 2)` per
cent of the range actually available to it. **That contrast is this book's
thesis in one sentence.** Read the first way the table says everything failed;
read the second it says the loss belongs to the data.

Excess sorts by what a method consumes. On the crease arm at target dimension
two the mean is `r signif(by_con$excess[by_con$consumes == "geodesic"], 3)` for
the one geodesic method,
`r signif(by_con$excess[by_con$consumes == "ambient"], 3)` for the ambient ones
and `r signif(by_con$excess[by_con$consumes == "neighbourhood"], 3)` for the
neighbourhood ones. Isomap consumes exactly what a crease pattern supplies
exactly [@tenenbaum2000isomap], and it is the method closest to the bound. That
ordering is measured over the whole sweep and all `r length(unique(grid$seed))`
seeds. The provisional version of it came from two values of $\theta$ in a
quick run that was never saved and put the ambient methods first — which is
exactly the reading standing rule 2 exists to prevent.

### Excess as a curve

```{r bench-fig-excess, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Mean excess over the floor at target dimension two, against each family's own difficulty parameter — the folding parameter on the left, the number of turns on the right. The vertical scales differ between panels and the two arms are matched on nothing, so this is a statement about the construction and not about which family is harder.", fig.alt="Two panels with independent axes. The left panel, crease product, plots excess over the floor against the folding parameter: three nearly flat curves for ambient, geodesic and neighbourhood methods sit between 0.01 and 0.10 until the folding parameter passes 0.8, where the ambient curve turns sharply upward and the geodesic one bends up more gently. The right panel, roll product, plots excess against the number of turns: three curves rise steadily together from about 0.72 to about 0.92 and stay within a hair of each other throughout."}
p2 <- ok[ok$d == 2L, ]
cur <- aggregate(excess ~ consumes + par + family, p2, mean)
cur$arm <- arm[cur$family]
ggplot2::ggplot(cur, ggplot2::aes(par, excess, colour = consumes,
                                  linetype = consumes, shape = consumes)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.9) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ arm, scales = "free") +
  viridis::scale_colour_viridis(discrete = TRUE, option = BOOK_VIRIDIS_OPTION,
                                end = 0.75) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "the family's own difficulty parameter",
                y = "mean excess over the floor") +
  theme_fold()
```

Figure \@ref(fig:bench-fig-excess) is the whole sweep.

```{r bench-curve, echo=TRUE}
crease_curve <- aggregate(cbind(excess, floor) ~ par, crease2, mean)
roll_curve   <- aggregate(cbind(excess, floor) ~ par, roll2, mean)
```

Two things read off it. On the crease arm the floor is
`r signif(crease_curve$floor[1], 3)` at every one of the nine folding
parameters — spread across the sweep exactly
`r diff(range(crease_curve$floor))` — while the excess climbs from
`r signif(min(crease_curve$excess), 3)` to
`r signif(max(crease_curve$excess), 3)`, almost all of it in the last two cells.
The bound is a property of the answer key and folding does not touch it; the
difficulty is entirely in the recovery. On the roll arm the floor *does* move,
from `r signif(max(roll_curve$floor), 3)` down to
`r signif(min(roll_curve$floor), 3)`, because winding more turns lengthens the
roll's arc-length coordinate and elongates its chart. Two arms, two different
relationships between difficulty and the bound, and neither is a defect.

### Why a benchmark stuck at intrinsic dimension 2 is not a serious benchmark

Everything above is unavailable on the book's main grid, and the reason is one
line of arithmetic. That grid's chart is two-dimensional and its target is
two-dimensional, so the `floor` column in it is identically zero — as
`irreducible_loss(sa, 2L)` returned above, for the same reason, in closed form.

That is not a defect in the grid and it is worth one sentence rather than a
footnote: **on the main grid every error is loss the method is responsible
for.** It is the cleanest possible reading, and it is available precisely
because the construction has no headroom in it.

But a benchmark that *only* ever has no headroom cannot ask the question this
chapter opened with. It cannot distinguish a method that discarded structure
from one that ran out of room, because there is never any room to run out of. It
cannot show what Figure \@ref(fig:bench-fig-dimension) shows — the crease arm's
methods hugging the bound at target dimensions one and two and pulling away from
it at three and four, which says where each method's loss comes from rather than
how large it is. And it cannot report a result as a ratio, because a ratio needs
both ends fixed and one end is nailed to zero.

The classical benchmarks are all in this position. A Swiss roll, an S-curve, a
severed sphere: two-dimensional charts, two-dimensional targets, floor zero
everywhere [@lee2007nonlinear]. Raising intrinsic dimension is the one move that
makes the bound bite, and doing it while keeping the answer key exact is what
`product_manifold()` is for. The product suite, not the main grid, carries the
argument.

## Diagnostics {#bench-diagnostics}

**Do not read the two arms as a difficulty comparison.** The crease arm is swept
over the folding parameter and the roll arm over turns; the two are matched on
nothing, and their floors differ by a factor of about
`r round(mean(crease2$floor) / mean(roll2$floor))` for reasons about how each
chart is parameterised rather than about how hard each object is. What the pair
supports is that the floor exists, is computable, is attained and is not beaten,
in both families. A claim that one family is harder needs matched difficulty and
does not live here.

**Rows that did not run are results.** Of the `r nrow(grid)` rows,
`r sum(grid$status == "unavailable")` are the autoencoder declaring itself
unavailable and `r sum(grid$status == "error")` are t-SNE refusing target
dimension four — the Barnes–Hut implementation accepts one, two or three, and
the `reason` column says so. Both are recorded rather than dropped, because a
missing row and a refused row look identical in an aggregate and mean opposite
things.

**The bound has no opinion about rank metrics.** `metric_floor()` bounds the
normalised Procrustes error and nothing else. Trustworthiness, continuity and
$Q_{NX}$ read rank order rather than distance, and an embedding sitting on this
floor may score better or worse on any of them than one well above it. That is
Chapter \@ref(evaluation)'s subject, not a defect here.

**One stale message.** `waterbomb()`'s error text still says the book ships two
families plus one negative result; it predates the Yoshimura's withdrawal and
was never revised. The count in this chapter is the correct one — one family,
two negative results — and the discrepancy is left visible rather than quietly
patched, because it is exactly the kind of stale count a registry keyed by
family name is supposed to catch and did not.

## Where it fails {#bench-limits}

**A product is not a curved four-manifold.** `product_manifold()` gives
intrinsic dimension four with an exact chart, and it gives it in the easiest
possible way: the factors are independent, their metrics do not interact, and
the chart's four coordinates come in two decoupled pairs. Nothing here models a
manifold whose curvature entangles its directions. The construction is for the
bound, and the bound needs only a chart of dimension greater than the target.

**The lift is linear.** What makes it a clean axis is also its limit. A random
orthonormal lift adds no correlated nuisance structure, no heteroscedastic noise
and no nearly redundant coordinates — none of the pathologies that make real
high-dimensional data hard [@chari2023specious; @lause2024elephant]. A method
that survives `lift()` has been shown insensitive to ambient dimension alone.

**The chart must be Euclidean.** The bound is an Eckart–Young residual and
needs the doubly-centred squared-distance matrix to be positive semi-definite.
It is here, by construction. A distance matrix handed in from elsewhere may not
be, and `chart_spectrum()` refuses that case rather than reporting a tail sum
that bounds nothing.

**The answer key is the chart only inside the paper.** Chart distance equals
geodesic distance only while the straight segment between two chart points stays
on the sheet, and a Miura's outline is not convex. The producer asserts a
chart-exit fraction of zero on every cell rather than trusting the sampling
default; where that assertion fails the answer key is wrong in the direction
that flatters every method.

**One family.** A benchmark built on a single pattern family cannot support
claims about pattern variety, and this book makes none. It can support claims
about a construction, and the suite's two arms are the evidence that the
construction is what the claims are about.

## Reproduce this {#bench-reproduce}

To add a family, write the constructor in `R/patterns.R` and the folding map in
`R/folding.R`, and let `tests/testthat/test-folding.R` decide whether it
qualifies: within-facet pairwise distances preserved to
`r format(TOL$isometry, scientific = TRUE)` across the sweep, flatness at
$\theta = 0$, an independent identity that was not built into the derivation,
and a mountain/valley assignment derived from the folded geometry rather than
asserted. A family that leaves a crease family flat fails the last of those,
which is how the Yoshimura was caught.

To build a product of your own, hand `product_manifold()` two `manifold_sample`
objects of equal size — they need not come from the same family, or from a
crease pattern at all — and score against `irreducible_loss()` rather than
against zero. `against_floor()` returns error, floor, excess and ratio together,
which is the form every result in Part III is reported in.

The suite itself is `scripts/run-product-grid.R`, which is run neither in CI nor
at render time: run it locally, commit the `.rds`, and let `read_run()` refuse
any chapter whose prose was written against a different one.

## Further reading {#bench-reading}

Miura's report [@miura1985method] introduces the one family this benchmark
folds, and Schenk and Guest [@schenk2013geometry] give the mechanics of folded
shells. Hull [@hull2020origametry] is the reference for what Kawasaki's and
Maekawa's conditions do and do not guarantee, Demaine and O'Rourke
[@demaine2007folding] for rigid foldability as a computational question, and
Lang [@lang2011origami] for the design side this chapter does not need.

On the measurement side, Eckart and Young [@eckart1936approximation] is the
approximation theorem the bound instantiates, Schönemann
[@schonemann1966procrustes] and Gower [@gower1975procrustes] fix the alignment
group it is stated over, and Torgerson [@torgerson1952mds] is where the chart
spectrum comes from. Balasubramanian and Schwartz [@balasubramanian2002isomap]
state the failure mode the folding parameter drives, and Lee and Verleysen
[@lee2007nonlinear] is the textbook treatment of the methods being measured.
Espadoto and colleagues [@espadoto2021survey] survey the benchmarking practice
this chapter argues with, and Machado and colleagues [@machado2025necessary]
make the case for evaluating the evaluators, which Chapter \@ref(evaluation)
takes up.
